catalog_quote: [p. 98, sec. 2.8.10 Tone and syllable prominence] There are no consistent stress patterns in Mian. However, syllables which are assigned H or HL from any of the tonal melodies H, HL, or LHL are more prominent that syllables which are assigned L. The phonetic manifestations are that they are longer and have high or falling pitch, e.g.: sékú [sɛ́ˑkʰúˑ] ‘bushknife’ ... Words with L tone are pronounced with no conspicuous change in pitch, e.g.: ibal [ìβàl] ‘dust’ ... [p. 70, sec. 2.8.2] Both nominals and verbs are lexically specified for one tonal melody and an accent which indicates where the tonal melody is to be inserted. The accent is the ‘anchor point’ for the melody ... There is a total of five tonal melodies (tonemes): L, H, LH, LHL, and HL. ... Generally, the accent for all stems is placed on the last stem syllable. Both nominals and verbs show accent placement which deviates form this rule. Nominals with a pharyngealized /aˤ/ as the nucleus of the first syllable; e.g. /LHkaˤwa/ ‘steel axe’ have the accent on the first syllable. Verbs fall into three classes: (i) unaccented, e.g. /fu/ ‘cook’, (ii) stem-accented, e.g. /LHLhɛla/ ‘break’ and (ii) off-stem-accented ones; e.g. /LHLlowon/ ‘eat’. In unaccented verbs L is spread over the whole word. ... [p. 90, sec. 2.8.9.2 Unaccented verbs] Phonetically, unaccented verbs do not have a prominent syllable, as far as higher fundamental frequency is concerned.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (500 PDF pages, text; p.1 is the Minerva Access cover sheet, so printed page = PDF page - 1, as the compilers states). extracted text of p.99 (printed 98) gives sec. 2.8.10 'Tone and syllable prominence' verbatim as quoted: 'There are no consistent stress patterns in Mian. However, syllables which are assigned H or HL from any of the tonal melodies H, HL, or LHL are more prominent that syllables which are assigned L. The phonetic manifestations are that they are longer and have high or falling pitch, e.g.: seku.. Words with L tone are pronounced with no conspicuous change in pitch, e.g.: ibal [dust]..' (including the source's own typo 'more prominent that'). p.71 (printed 70),…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mian is a word-tone language: each word carries one of five tonemes (L, H, LH, LHL, HL) anchored at a lexically specified 'accent' that by default sits on the last stem syllable (initial syllable if it contains pharyngealized /aˤ/; verbs are unaccented, stem-accented, or off-stem-accented, the last shifting the anchor one syllable right under suffixation). There is no independent stress system: perceived prominence (extra length, high/falling pitch) simply falls on whichever syllables receive H or HL from the melody, and all-L words have no prominent syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; prominence is a by-product of tone, not a metrical system.
new_statements.exceptions: Nominals with pharyngealized /aˤ/ in the first syllable take initial accent (kaˤwá 'steel axe', p.57, 78); off-stem-accented verbs shift the accent to the syllable after the stem when suffixed or auxiliary-compounded (p.70, 93); Future suffixes /aˈmab/, /oˈmab/ are inherently accented (p.95); benefactive applicative /b/ makes unaccented verbs stem-accented with LHL (p.96); unaccented (all-L) verbs 'do not have a prominent syllable' (p.90).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of tone/accent assignment is the phonological word including affixes and most clitics; nominal and verbal compounds count as one phonological word with one melody and one accent (p.25). Statements concern citation/word forms; vowel length also varies with syllable count (monosyllable > accented syllable of disyllable > of trisyllable, p.53-54).
new_statements.identity_note: Fedden's description is explicitly based on the eastern dialect (East Mianmin, villages around Mianmin airstrip, Gubil, Fiak, Hotmin; thesis p. 28: 'The language description presented in this thesis is based on the eastern dialect') = Glottolog mian1256 (dialect mian1257 'Mianmin'). The western variety (West Mianmin / Wagarabai / Suganga, around Yapsiei) is a separate Glottolog languoid suga1249 [sug] and is not the object of the description.

new_statements.quote: [p. 25, 4.3.2 Stress] Stress is non-contrastive in the Mianmin language. If there is only one high tone /´/ or high falling /ˆ/ in the word, it will take the stress. Should there be more than one high /´/ tone or high glide /ˆ/ they will receive equal stress. If all syllables in a word are low tone /`/ or low rising /ˇ/ each syllable receives equal stress. [p. 25, 4.3.3.1] There are four emic tones: high /´/, high falling /ˆ/, low /`/ and low rising /ˇ/. [p. 29, 5.3] High and low tones occur on any syllable in a word while high falling and low rising only occur on the final syllable of a word. High falling also does not occur on one syllable words.

new_statements.relation_note: Same conclusion as the catalog's Fedden 2007 statement (no consistent/contrastive stress; prominence falls on high-toned syllables; all-low words have no prominent syllable). It predates Fedden and uses a different tonal analysis (four syllable tones vs Fedden's five word-level melodies anchored by an accent), so it adds an independent 1974 confirmation rather than new placement detail; it does not state Fedden's default last-stem-syllable accent.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mianmin is analysed as a syllable-tone language with four tonemes (high, high falling, low, low rising; the last two only word-finally). Stress is explicitly non-contrastive and is a by-product of tone: the one syllable bearing high or high-falling tone takes the stress; if several syllables are high/high-falling they are equally stressed; a word whose syllables are all low or low-rising has all syllables equally stressed (i.e. no prominent syllable). No positional (initial/penult/final) stress rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; multiple high-toned syllables in one word are said to 'receive equal stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. Tone: high falling and low rising occur only on the final syllable, high falling never on monosyllables; pitch perturbation across word boundaries (sec. 4.3.4) changes tones in phrases, with one exception (a high-low disyllable is never perturbed).
new_statements.identity_note: Smith & Weston were the SIL team at the Mianmin station (eastern dialect area), the same variety Fedden describes (East Mianmin = mian1256/mian1257); the scanned excerpt itself names only 'the Mianmin language' and does not specify a dialect. archive.org labels the Rosetta item 'Mian' (mpt). Note for the bibliography: Glottolog record 152082 for 'Mianmin Phonemes and Tonemes' carries the page range 35-142, which belongs to 'Notes on Mianmin grammar'; the scan shows the phonology paper's own pagination runs from about p. 5 (chart of phonemes on p. 6, Stress on p. 25, Orthography pp. 29-30). The excerpt found on archive.org is partial (pp. 6, 17-29, plus separate Rosetta items for orthography pp. 29-30 and a text pp. 51-52); sec. 3.2.1 on length is not in the excerpt.

sources.note: Mian is a word-tone language (5 tonemes L, H, LH, LHL, HL assigned to the phonological word) with a lexically specified accent = anchor point for the melody, by default on the last stem syllable (p.70; p.57), initial if first syllable has pharyngealized /a/; verbs unaccented / stem-accented / off-stem-accented. Sec. 2.8.10 (p.98): 'There are no consistent stress patterns in Mian'; H/HL-toned syllables are more prominent (longer, high/falling pitch); all-L words have no prominent syllable.
